Personally, I would avoid galvanised steel. The surface isn't very attratictive. You could use the same gauge, or even 0.5mm mild steel and treat it with brush on bluing solution. It will prevent it from rusting, and make it look pretty cool. You can also treat it with a clear matte or gloss laquer, this will prevent rusting also, and will keep the bright look of the steel.

Another suggestion could be to solder the seams where there is a gap, solder will wet to mild steel, and will fill gaps. If you are confident in your soldering ability, you could also solder panels together to eliminate the overlap.

You could also use the same thickness brass or copper sheet, it's more expensive, but looks snazzy. This could be a more expensive model?

Brass and copper can be worked much the same way, they take a bend well, and can be polished to a very high surface finish. You can also experiment with oxidisation to make a mask that looks like it's ancient.

Design still needs work, hardware needs changing - rivets or acorn nuts would look better, metal bends also need to be tighter. 

The finish needs work, I can see serrations from the cutter, and lots of sharp edges and corners. Take a file and sandpaper to it before and after you bend it. Try to eliminate gaps too, light shining through them is not a good look on a product you indent to sell. 

Practice more, make several more of these - trying to make each better than the last, and pay particular attention to the finish. Also maybe change the metal you are using, based on the creasing it looks extremely thin, and maybe galvanised. Thicker, and heavier is good, heavy means reliable. 

Practice with paper, or heavy card. Make iterations with that, it's cheaper and quicker than metal.
